title: Indexes for text, time and vectors
goal: By the end you can say why a B+tree only answers questions about one sort order, and explain the index built for each other shape of question: posting lists in Lucene segments for words, time chunks and rollups for time, geohashes, R-trees and H3 cells for maps, and HNSW and DiskANN graphs for vectors, with what each one gives up.

warmup.q: A support agent types "Nrthwind bikes" into the merchant search. The service runs `SELECT * FROM merchant WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%nrthwind%'` on Oracle, with a B-tree index on `name`. What happens?
options: The index finds Northwind Bikes, because LIKE uses the index
Nothing is found, and Oracle reads every merchant to find out
Northwind Bikes is found, ranked first
Oracle rejects the query: LIKE needs a prefix
warmup.why: A B-tree keeps whole names in order, so it can only jump to a known prefix; a leading `%` means reading every row. And `LIKE` matches characters exactly: "nrthwind" is not in "northwind", so even the full scan finds nothing, and nothing would be ranked anyway. Words in any order, typos and ranking need an inverted index with fuzzy matching.

sections.h: Words: an inverted index maps every word to the documents that contain it
sections.body:
Lesson 7's B+tree keeps one sort order. It answers "equal to this key", "between these keys" and "starts with this prefix", and nothing else. Support needs to find a merchant from whatever a caller says: "the Northwind bike place", or a typo like "Nrthwind". A B+tree index on `name` keeps whole strings in order, so `WHERE lower(name) LIKE '%bike%'` reads every row, and it has no idea which match is best.

Version 1 scans: read every name and check whether it contains the words. With 2 million merchants, every keystroke reads 2 million names, and the results come back in no useful order.

Version 2 turns the data round. When a document is indexed, an analyzer splits its text into tokens (lower-cased words, here) and the index records, for every token, the list of documents that contain it, with how often. That list is a **posting list**, and the whole structure is an inverted index: from words to documents, the opposite of a document holding its words. A query goes through the same analyzer, reads one posting list per query word and merges them. The cost follows the length of those lists, not the number of merchants. The first stepper builds it for five names.

**Every index in this lesson is the same deal as lesson 7's B+tree: a second copy of the data, organised for one shape of question and paid for on every write.** The shapes are words to documents, time to buckets, a place to what's near it, and a vector to its nearest neighbours. Choosing whole stores built around these indexes was the Data models track's job; this lesson opens the indexes themselves.

Version 3 ranks. Most search engines use BM25. For each query word in a document it adds `idf x tf / (tf + k1 x (1 - b + b x length / average length))`. A rare word counts more than a common one: idf, the inverse document frequency. A word that appears twice counts more than once, with diminishing returns: k1 = 1.2 caps it. A match in a short name counts more than one in a long description: b = 0.75 scales by length. The analyzer must be the same at index time and query time, and typos need fuzzy matching, which accepts terms one or two edits away.

How do you add documents to sorted posting lists? The way lesson 5's LSM tree adds keys. Lucene, the library inside OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, buffers new documents in memory and writes them out as a new immutable segment: a small inverted index of its own. A search reads every segment and merges the answers. A refresh writes a segment, every second by default in OpenSearch, and that's when a new document becomes searchable. A delete only marks the document in a bitmap; an update is a delete plus an add. In the background a merge policy combines segments, like compaction: Lucene 10.3's `TieredMergePolicy` merges segments of about the same size, up to 10 at a time, aims for about 8 per size tier, and drops deleted documents as it rewrites. PostgreSQL's GIN index is an inverted index too, as the compare block shows.

sections.h: Time: cut it into chunks and buckets, keep the summaries, drop the rest
sections.body:
Every card authorization records how long the card issuer took to answer. At 2,000 authorizations a second that's 173 million points a day, and the questions have a shape: the last hour's latency for one merchant, a 5-minute chart for the past week, a daily figure for the past year. Writes only ever append at the current time. Reads ask for a range of time, mostly recent. Old points matter only as summaries.

Time is one dimension, so a B+tree can find a range of it. That's version 1: one table with a B+tree index on time. Inserts land at the right edge of the index, which is fine. Then retention: deleting a day of old rows is 173 million single-row deletes, each leaving a dead row version behind for VACUUM to clean up (the Transactions track's lesson on MVCC explains why). And the yearly chart reads about 63 billion rows to draw 365 points.

Version 2 partitions by time. TimescaleDB, a PostgreSQL extension, turns a table into a hypertable: one table to you, a chunk per time interval underneath (one per hour in the Try-it). A query for 09:00 to 10:00 opens only the chunk that holds that hour; the planner leaves the other 23 out. Retention drops whole chunks, which deletes files instead of rows. That's how `add_retention_policy` works.

Version 3 downsamples, the "time to buckets" part of the picture. Cut time into fixed buckets with `time_bucket`, and keep per bucket the count, the sum, the min and the max. Keep sums and counts rather than averages, because they add up: twelve 5-minute buckets roll up into an exact hour, while an average of averages weights a quiet five minutes the same as a busy one. A continuous aggregate keeps those summaries up to date as rows arrive, which makes it a materialized view maintained incrementally, lesson 12's subject. Then the raw points can expire after days while the hourly summaries stay for years.

TimescaleDB keeps its name, though the company renamed itself Tiger Data in June 2025. InfluxDB 3 does the same job on Apache Arrow and Parquet files, and the Cassandra tables bucketed by day in the Data models track are the same idea done by hand.

sections.h: Maps: one sort order can't hold two dimensions
sections.body:
The risk team asks for every card terminal inside a box around a shop that reported skimming, about 11 km by 10 km around Amsterdam. Each terminal has a latitude and a longitude. Try lesson 7's tool first: a B+tree on `(lat, lon)`. It sorts by latitude, and by longitude only among equal latitudes, the column-order rule from lesson 7. So the box's latitude range is one stretch of the index, a band that runs across the whole width of the map, and the longitude condition is checked entry by entry inside it. In the Try it, 1,000,000 terminals spread over Europe put 4,098 entries in the band and 11 in the box. Make the map twice as wide and the band doubles; the answer doesn't.

Version 2 squeezes two dimensions into one. A **geohash** halves the longitude range and records which half the point is in (one bit), then does the same for latitude, and so on, alternating. Every 5 bits become one base-32 character. Dam Square is `u173z`: a cell about 4.9 km tall and 3 km wide, and every point inside it has a geohash that starts with `u173z`. Points close on the map mostly share a prefix, so an ordinary B+tree on the geohash string answers "near here" with a prefix range. Mostly is the catch: two terminals 10 metres apart on either side of a cell edge can differ from an early character. The corners of the Try it's box are `u173t` and `u17d0`. So a search also reads the neighbouring cells.

Version 3 stops sorting and groups instead. An **R-tree** keeps, in each node, the bounding rectangle of everything below it. A search descends into every child whose rectangle overlaps the box, the way a B+tree descends into the child whose key range holds the key. Nearby points share a leaf, whatever their order. PostgreSQL builds R-trees on GiST (generalized search tree), a framework where an index type supplies five methods, among them `consistent` (could this entry match the query?), `union` (the rectangle around these entries) and `picksplit` (how to split a full node). The built-in `point_ops` and PostGIS's geometry indexes are R-trees built this way. In the Try it the GiST index answered the box from 8 pages, and "the 5 terminals nearest to Dam Square" from 12, a question a B+tree can't serve at all: without the GiST index, PostgreSQL computed the distance to all 1,000,000 terminals.

Version 4 trades exact shapes for a fixed grid. Uber's H3 divides the globe into hexagons at 16 resolutions: 122 cells at resolution 0 (110 hexagons and 12 pentagons), and 7 children per cell at each step down, so a resolution-9 cell is about 0.1 km². Every terminal gets a cell id, a 64-bit integer, and "terminals per cell" becomes a GROUP BY on an integer column. All six neighbours of a hexagon are the same distance away, which makes heat maps and "everything within two rings" simple. H3 is for counting and joining by area; for exact boxes and distances, use the R-tree.

sections.h: Vectors: find the nearest neighbours by walking a graph, approximately
sections.body:
A customer writes: "charged twice for one bike rental". Support wants past disputes like it, by meaning, not by shared words. "Duplicate charge, scooter hire" should match even though it shares no word with the first. An inverted index can't do that. An embedding can: a model turns each text into a vector, a list of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, placed so that texts with similar meanings land close together. Finding similar disputes becomes finding the nearest vectors. Close means a small distance: Euclidean (L2), cosine or inner product, written `<->`, `<=>` and `<#>` in pgvector. Use the one your embedding model was trained for.

Version 1 is exact: compute the distance from the query to every vector and keep the k smallest. The Try-it does that over 100,000 vectors of 32 numbers: 2,138 pages, about 8 ms. With 50 million disputes of 1,536 numbers each, it's 77 billion multiply-adds per query.

Version 2 would be an index from the last section, and neither works. A B+tree needs one sort order. An R-tree's bounding boxes, in hundreds of dimensions, overlap almost any query, so the search opens nearly every node.

Version 3 gives up exactness. Build a graph in which every vector links to some of its nearest neighbours, and search it by walking: start somewhere, move to whichever neighbour is closer to the query, stop when none is. HNSW, from a 2016 paper by Malkov and Yashunin, adds layers like a skip list: a few vectors in the top layer with long links, more in each layer below, every vector in the bottom one, where the search keeps a beam of the `ef` best candidates. The second stepper walks it. Three numbers tune it. `m` is the number of links per vector (16 in pgvector), `ef_construction` the beam while building (64), and `hnsw.ef_search` the beam while searching (40). The price is **recall**, the share of the true nearest neighbours the search returns. In the Try-it the index read 654 pages in under a millisecond, with recall@10 of about 0.89 at `ef_search = 10` and 1.0 at 40. The index took 41 MB for 17 MB of vectors, and every hop is a random read, so HNSW wants its graph in memory.

Filters are the trap. pgvector applies a WHERE clause after the index walk: the walk finds `ef_search` candidates, then the filter drops the ones that don't match. With a filter that keeps about 1 row in 11, `LIMIT 10` returned 4 rows on average in the Try-it, as pgvector's README predicts for a 10% filter. No error, just fewer rows. Since 0.8.0, `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` makes the scan keep walking until enough rows pass, up to `hnsw.max_scan_tuples` (20,000): 10 of 10.

At a billion vectors the graph no longer fits in RAM. **DiskANN** (Subramanya and colleagues, 2019) keeps the graph on SSD and compressed vectors in memory. On one machine with 64 GB of RAM it indexed a billion points and served over 5,000 queries a second with under 3 ms mean latency at 95% recall@1. Compressed means quantization: scalar quantization stores each number in fewer bits (pgvector's `halfvec` uses 16 instead of 32, binary quantization keeps 1 bit), and product quantization (Jégou and colleagues, 2011) cuts a vector into pieces and replaces each piece by the id of its nearest centroid, so 128 numbers become 8 bytes. Distances on compressed vectors are rough, so engines re-rank: fetch extra candidates with the small vectors, then sort them by the exact distance.

analogy: Think of the same pile of merchant files kept for different questions. The B+tree is the cabinet sorted by name: perfect for "the file called Northwind", useless for "every file that mentions bikes". The inverted index is the index at the back of a book, from each word to the pages it appears on. The time chunks are one drawer per month, emptied into a yearly summary sheet before the drawer is thrown out. The R-tree is a map cut into labelled envelopes, each envelope holding the shops of one area, nested inside bigger envelopes. HNSW is a city where every house knows a few neighbours and a motorway gets you to the right district before you walk the last streets. The analogy breaks on cost: a paper index is written once, while every one of these is updated on every write, and the approximate ones can quietly hand you the wrong shop.
in_your_world: Look at what your payments platform already asks. Merchant search is probably a `LIKE` against Oracle or a search cluster someone set up years ago; posting lists and BM25 are what make it rank, and Lucene's segments are why a new merchant appears a second later. Authorization latency lands in a metrics system that is a time-series store with chunks, rollups and retention. A fraud rule such as "terminals within 5 km of a reported skimmer" is an R-tree query, and "card-present payments per hexagon" is an H3 GROUP BY. Dispute similarity is the obvious first use of vectors: embed the customer's text, keep it in pgvector next to the dispute rows, and check recall with the filters your agents actually use, such as one merchant's disputes. Oracle has its own versions of each: Oracle Text for words, R-tree indexes in Oracle Spatial, and vector indexes in its AI Vector Search.
mistake: The most common mistake with these indexes is trusting an approximate search with a filter: `WHERE merchant_id = ? ORDER BY embedding <-> ? LIMIT 10` on an HNSW index. It works in testing, where the filter matches most rows. In production one merchant owns 2% of the disputes, the index walk collects 40 candidates, the filter keeps one or none, and the screen shows "no similar disputes" for a merchant that has hundreds. Nothing errors, so nobody notices. People expect a WHERE clause to behave the way it does on a B+tree, where the filter never changes how many rows LIMIT can reach. The fix: turn on iterative scans (`hnsw.iterative_scan`), or give a very selective filter its own index (a partial index per large merchant, or partitioning), or search the few matching rows exactly; then measure recall with the real filters, against an exact search with index scans off.

compare.note: Both are inverted indexes over the same five names, and both answers are real output (PostgreSQL 18 in a throwaway container, OpenSearch from the Try-it). `plainto_tsquery` requires every word, so PostgreSQL returns only M-0042; ask for either word with `websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'northwind or bikes')` and it returns four rows, M-0044 included, because its english stemmer turns "Bike" and "Bikes" into the same lexeme. `ts_rank` is not BM25: it ignores how rare a word is across the table. worked.title: Compute a geohash by hand, then in Kotlin

steps.say: Start with Dam Square, latitude 52.373 and longitude 4.893. Each step halves a range and records which half the point is in: 1 for the upper half, 0 for the lower. Longitude goes first, then the two alternate.

Five bits make one base-32 character. The alphabet is the digits and the letters without a, i, l and o, so 11010 = 26 is `u`. The next five bits, 00001, are `1`: the cell `u1` covers latitude 50.6 to 56.3 and longitude 0 to 11.25.
Keep going to 25 bits and the geohash is `u173z`, a cell 0.044 degrees on each side: 4.9 km north to south and, at this latitude, 3.0 km east to west. Six characters would be about 610 m by 750 m.
The same steps in Kotlin. Each loop turn produces one bit; every fifth bit closes a character.
steps.code:
fun geohash(lat: Double, lon: Double, chars: Int): String {
    val base32 = "0123456789bcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz"
    val latRange = doubleArrayOf(-90.0, 90.0)
    val lonRange = doubleArrayOf(-180.0, 180.0)
    val out = StringBuilder()
    var bits = 0
    var nBits = 0
    var lonTurn = true                                   // longitude first, then alternate
    while (out.length < chars) {
        val range = if (lonTurn) lonRange else latRange
        val v = if (lonTurn) lon else lat
        val mid = (range[0] + range[1]) / 2
        bits = bits shl 1
        if (v >= mid) { bits = bits or 1; range[0] = mid } else range[1] = mid
        lonTurn = !lonTurn
        if (++nBits == 5) { out.append(base32[bits]); bits = 0; nBits = 0 }   // 5 bits: one character
    }
    return out.toString()
}

geohash(52.373, 4.893, 5)   // "u173z"

drill.title: BM25 and a rollup by hand
drill.prompt: Without looking: (a) write BM25's score for one query term in one document, and say in a phrase what idf, k1 and b each do; (b) two documents contain "northwind" once each, one is 2 tokens long and the other 7, the average is 4.2: which ranks first, and why; (c) two 5-minute buckets have (count 99, sum 9,900) and (count 1, sum 900): what is the hourly average, and what would averaging the averages give?

answer.src:
(a) idf(t) * tf / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * len / avglen))
    idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)): rare terms count more
    k1 (1.2): saturates repeats, so the 10th occurrence adds little
    b (0.75): how much a long document is penalised for its length
(b) the 2-token one: same tf and idf, smaller length -> smaller denominator
    (0.506 against 0.313 in the lesson's five merchants)
(c) (9,900 + 900) / (99 + 1) = 108
    averaging the averages: (100 + 900) / 2 = 500, wrong, because it weights
    one quiet bucket like 99 busy ones. Keep count and sum, never the average.

recap: A B+tree answers questions about one sort order. Every index in this lesson is another copy of the data, organised for a different shape of question and paid for on every write.

An inverted index maps each term to a posting list of documents; BM25 ranks by rarity, saturated frequency and length. Lucene writes it as immutable segments that a refresh opens and a merge policy compacts, an LSM tree again.
Time-series stores partition by time into chunks, keep count, sum, min and max per bucket, roll buckets up, and drop whole old chunks. Never average averages.

Two dimensions break a B+tree on (lat, lon), which walks a whole latitude band. Geohashes turn a cell into a prefix, R-trees (GiST in PostgreSQL) group points under bounding boxes and answer nearest-neighbour queries, and H3 hexagons give every place an integer cell id.

HNSW walks a layered graph with a beam: `m` 16, `ef_construction` 64, `ef_search` 40 in pgvector. It trades recall for speed, wants its graph in memory, and applies filters after the walk, so a selective filter returns too few rows unless iterative scans are on.
At billion scale, DiskANN keeps the graph on SSD and quantized vectors in RAM; scalar, binary and product quantization shrink vectors, and a re-rank with exact distances recovers the recall.

quiz.q: A merchant named "City Bike Rental" doesn't show up for the query "bikes" in an index that uses OpenSearch's `standard` analyzer. Why?
options: The document hasn't been refreshed yet
The standard analyzer doesn't stem, so `bike` and `bikes` are different terms with different posting lists
BM25 gave it a score of zero because the name is short
Single-word queries need fuzzy matching
quiz.why: Matching happens on terms, and the standard analyzer only splits and lower-cases. `bikes` has its own posting list, which doesn't contain M-0044. A stemming analyzer such as `english`, used at both index and query time, maps both to `bike`. BM25 only ranks documents that matched; it never zeroes a match out.

quiz.q: A table holds 2 million terminals across Europe with a B+tree on `(lat, lon)`. A query asks for terminals in a 10 km box around Lyon. What does the index scan read?
options: Only the entries inside the box, because both columns are in the index
Every entry in the index, because two ranges can't use a B+tree
Every entry whose latitude falls in the box's latitude range, across the whole width of the map, checking longitude one entry at a time
Only the entries whose longitude is in range, because the second column is checked first
quiz.why: The index is sorted by latitude first and by longitude only among equal latitudes, so the latitude range is one contiguous stretch: a band from Portugal to Romania. Longitude is tested inside the scan on each entry. That is why the Try it's B+tree walked 4,098 entries for 11 rows, and why an R-tree or a geohash prefix does better. It does use the index, so a full index scan is wrong too.

quiz.q: A latency table holds 13 months of raw points, and you must keep only 30 days of raw data. Why does a time-series store drop chunks instead of running `DELETE ... WHERE time < now() - interval '30 days'`?
options: DELETE isn't allowed on a hypertable
Dropping a chunk removes a whole file in one step; DELETE marks hundreds of millions of rows dead and leaves the cleanup to VACUUM
DELETE would also remove the continuous aggregate
Chunks are compressed, so rows can't be found
quiz.why: Because data is partitioned by time, everything older than the cutoff sits in whole chunks, and dropping one is a file deletion. A row-by-row DELETE leaves a dead version per row for VACUUM to clean up later, which the Transactions track's lesson on MVCC explains. DELETE does work on a hypertable; it's just the expensive way.

quiz.q: `SELECT id FROM disputes WHERE merchant_id = 42 ORDER BY embedding <-> :q LIMIT 10` uses pgvector's HNSW index with default settings. Merchant 42 owns 10% of the disputes. Why does it often return only about 4 rows?
options: The index walk collects `ef_search` = 40 candidates first, and the WHERE clause runs afterwards and keeps about 10% of them
Merchant 42 has only 4 disputes near the query
LIMIT is applied before ORDER BY on an approximate index
The HNSW index skips rows that were updated since it was built
quiz.why: pgvector filters after the index scan. The walk returns its 40 best candidates by distance, the filter keeps the ones for merchant 42, and about 4 survive; LIMIT can't ask for more. Merchant 42 may have hundreds of close disputes the walk never reached. Iterative scans (`hnsw.iterative_scan`) keep walking until enough rows pass, and a larger `ef_search` also helps at a cost.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: you delete 30% of the documents in a search index, and its size on disk doesn't shrink. A day later it is much smaller. What happened?
options: The deletes were queued in memory and written a day later
The operating system freed its page cache
The index was rebuilt from the database overnight
Segments are immutable: a delete only marks the document, and the space came back when the merge policy rewrote those segments, as compaction drops tombstoned keys in an LSM tree
quiz.why: Lucene never edits a segment in place. A delete sets a bit in a per-segment bitmap, searches skip the document, and its bytes stay until a merge copies the live documents into a new segment and drops the old ones. That is lesson 5's LSM compaction: tombstones and old versions vanish only when files are rewritten. Lucene's default merge policy also tries to keep deleted documents under about 20% of the index.

flashcards.back: For one term, the list of documents that contain it, with how often. An inverted index is a dictionary of terms to posting lists.

flashcards.front: What is a Lucene segment, and when does a new document become searchable?
flashcards.back: An immutable mini inverted index. New documents are buffered and become searchable when a refresh writes them as a segment (every second by default in OpenSearch); merges combine segments later.

flashcards.front: What do a hypertable's chunks buy you?
flashcards.back: Queries over a time range open only the chunks for that range, and retention drops whole chunks instead of deleting rows.

flashcards.front: Why does a B+tree on (lat, lon) do badly on a small box?
flashcards.back: It sorts by latitude first, so it walks every entry in the box's latitude band, across the whole map, and checks longitude one entry at a time.

flashcards.front: How does an R-tree search a box?
flashcards.back: Each node stores the bounding rectangle of everything below it; the search descends only into children whose rectangle overlaps the box. PostgreSQL builds R-trees on GiST.

flashcards.front: pgvector's HNSW settings and their defaults?
flashcards.back: `m` 16 links per vector, `ef_construction` 64 (beam while building), `hnsw.ef_search` 40 (beam while searching; higher means better recall, slower queries).

flashcards.front: Why can a filtered HNSW query return fewer rows than its LIMIT?
flashcards.back: The filter runs after the index walk. With `ef_search` 40 and a 10% filter, about 4 candidates survive. `hnsw.iterative_scan` keeps walking until enough pass.

terms.plain: A map from each term to the documents that contain it; the core of every search engine and of PostgreSQL's GIN index.
In Lucene, an immutable part of the index written at each refresh and merged with others in the background.
TimescaleDB's time-partitioned table: one table to queries, one chunk per time interval underneath.
A string made by interleaving halvings of longitude and latitude, so nearby points usually share a prefix.
A tree whose nodes store bounding rectangles; a search opens only the children that overlap the query. GiST is PostgreSQL's framework for building one.
Hierarchical navigable small world: a layered graph of vectors searched greedily from the top layer down, with a beam at the bottom.
The share of the true k nearest neighbours an approximate search returns; 1.0 means it found them all.
Storing vectors in fewer bits (16-bit, 1-bit, or product-quantized codes) so more fit in memory, at some cost in accuracy.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why we can't add ordinary B+tree indexes for merchant search, the skimming map and "similar disputes". Explain what each of those three questions needs from an index, and what each special index gives up.
explain_back.answer: A B+tree keeps one sort order, so it only helps with equality, ranges and prefixes on that order. Merchant search needs words in any position, typos and ranking: an inverted index keeps a posting list per word, so a query reads a few lists instead of every name, and BM25 ranks by rarity and length. It's written in immutable segments, so new merchants show up after a refresh, and deletes take space until a merge. The skimming map needs two dimensions at once: a B+tree on latitude and longitude walks a whole latitude band across the map, while an R-tree (GiST in PostgreSQL) groups nearby terminals under bounding boxes and reads only the boxes that overlap, and it can also find the nearest terminals. Similar disputes need nearest neighbours among embeddings with hundreds of dimensions, where neither a sort order nor bounding boxes help. HNSW walks a graph and gives up a little recall for a large speed-up, needs its graph in memory, and applies filters after the walk, so a filtered query can come back short unless iterative scans are on. Each one is an extra structure every write must update, so I'd add them in PostgreSQL first (full-text search, GiST, pgvector) and measure.

deeper.body:
Posting lists are compressed hard, because most of a search index is posting lists. Lucene stores document ids as gaps from the previous id, packs those small numbers into blocks of bits, and keeps skip data so that intersecting a rare term's list with a common one can jump ahead instead of reading every entry. A query for two words is closer to a merge join with skips than to a scan.

Percentiles don't roll up the way sums do. You can't combine two buckets' p99 into the hour's p99. Time-series systems keep a small mergeable sketch per bucket instead, such as a t-digest or a fixed-boundary histogram. If an SLA is written as a percentile, check that your store keeps a sketch rather than a stored percentile.

Space-filling curves are the general idea behind geohashes. The Z-order curve that bit interleaving traces jumps at every cell boundary; a Hilbert curve visits cells in an order where consecutive cells always touch, so a box maps to fewer, longer ranges of the one-dimensional key. Bkd-trees, which Lucene uses for numbers and geo points, split space by alternating dimensions like a k-d tree and store the leaves in blocks on disk.

HNSW isn't the only approximate index. IVF (inverted file) indexes cluster the vectors around centroids, and a search compares the query with the centroids and scans only the nearest few clusters (`ivfflat.lists`, a good start being rows / 1000, and `ivfflat.probes`, default 1, in pgvector). They build faster and use less memory than HNSW, and usually need more tuning for the same recall. Graph indexes can also fail on strongly clustered data: while this lesson's Try-it was being written, vectors in 200 tight, well-separated clusters left recall stuck at 0.90 even at `ef_search = 200`, because two queries never reached their cluster from the entry point. More links per vector (`m`) is the usual remedy.

Every index in this lesson can also live outside your main database, in a search cluster or a vector database. Then it is a copy that lags, and it has to be fed from the system of record without writing twice; the Derived data track builds that properly.
